entries.title: Is Germany's eight-hour workday under threat?
entries.summary: Would you work 12 hours straight? The CDU/CSU and SPD are locked in a dispute over reforms to the Working Hours Act. Workplace flexibility, collective bargaining agreements and worker protection rules are at stake.
entries.content:
Germany

Is Germany's eight-hour workday under threat?

October 18, 2026

Would you work 12 hours straight? The CDU/CSU and SPD are locked in a dispute over reforms to the Working Hours Act. Workplace flexibility, collective bargaining agreements and worker protection rules are at stake.

The town of Leuna, in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, is one of the country's largest chemical industry hub, where more than 100 companies have established operations. Among them is the Finnish biotechnology group UPM, which has recently built a biorefinery for wood-based chemicals in Leuna. It's now hiring.

One of the job listings is for a chemical technician to oversee the rollout of new facilities. But to qualify, candidates must be willing to work 12-hour shifts. Is that legal? According to German law, standard working hours are limited to eight hours per day. It is permissible to extend this to ten hours, provided that workers receive compensatory time off for the overtime, and there must be at least 11 hours of rest between two shifts.

Twelve-hour shifts? What German law permits

Business associations and the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU) parties have long called for these rules to be made more flexible.

Rainer Dulger, president of the Confederation of German Employers' Associations (BDA), points to the European Working Time Directive, which allows for a maximum weekly working time of 48 hours. "The allowance is being taken advantage of almost everywhere else — except here," Dulger told the dpa news agency in August.

Companies say they often find the existing rules too rigid, particularly in industries with seasonal fluctuations — such as tourism — or in project-based work, or during irregular peaks in workload, such as in the restaurant industry. They could deploy their staff more efficiently, says Dulger: "The Working Hours Act dates back to the era of fax machines and rotary-dial phones. It knows nothing of laptops or daycare hours."

CDU and SPD divided on working hours

In their 2025 coalition agreement, the CDU/CSU and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) agreed to reform the Working Hours Act. "In keeping with the European Working Time Directive, we want to allow for a maximum weekly rather than daily working time — also and especially to promote a better work-life balance," the agreement said.

The SPD would have preferred to leave the law unchanged, but had to accept the conservative parties' plans. The Social Democrats pointed out that longer working hours are already permitted in exceptional cases, such as in emergency services, the health care sector and security services. Workers in power plants, refineries and the chemical industry are also allowed to work up to 12 hours at a time.

A surprise for Chancellor Friedrich Merz

Even Chancellor Friedrich Merz himself seemed unaware of this exception until quite recently. After visiting the UPM refinery in Leuna in September, he recounted to business leaders at the German Employers' Day in Berlin that he was "completely surprised" to learn that the facilities operate on a continuous 12-hour shift schedule, thanks to the approval of the works council.

Merz recounted the shift supervisor describing the work schedule as "really great" — with three-day work weeks. "He said we have plenty of time for our families — it's a great way to organize things." Merz went on to conclude that this demonstrates the benefits of relaxing the Working Hours Act.

"Working more than eight hours is not exploitation. Rather, it can be a good opportunity to organize working hours more flexibly — both for businesses and for the people working there," the chancellor said. "We should do it."

SPD agrees to longer working hours, but with conditions

But there is resistance from within the SPD and from trade unions opposed to amending the Working Hours Act. The trade union Verdi argues that significantly longer workdays would have negative consequences for employees' health and would disadvantage people with family and caregiving responsibilities. In certain industries, employees could also be put under pressure to accept longer shifts.

An initial reform draft was drawn up in June 2026 by the Labor and Social Affairs Ministry, headed at the time by Bärbel Bas, an SPD politician who has since resigned for personal reasons.

The draft includes some conditions, including a collective bargaining agreement between employers and unions if any schedule changes were made, as well as health and safety regulations, and working hours to be tracked electronically.

Dispute over collective bargaining rights and worker protection

Annika Klose, spokesperson for labor and social policy for the SPD parliamentary group, explained the thinking behind the idea. Flexibility, she said, is "not a one-way street." The coalition agreement explicitly aims to promote a better balance between family and work. "So that it's sometimes possible to take your child to football practice in the afternoon and then continue working afterward — but not that my boss tells me against my will: 'You're working the shift from 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. tomorrow.'"

The CDU/CSU immediately rejected the draft. Businesses were also up in arms. "This draft must be withdrawn and completely revised," demanded Dulger in a statement, saying it was "steeped in mistrust." The German Confederation of Skilled Crafts (ZDH) spoke of a "breach of the commitments agreed to in the coalition agreement." The reform has been on hold ever since.

Why the reform stalled

At the Employers' Day event, Merz held out the prospect of progress. "This is indeed long overdue. I believe we can accomplish this relatively quickly and create flexibility in the labor market."

It remains to be seen, however, whether the new SPD Labor Minister, Alexander Schweitzer, shares this view. In early October, his party released a paper on reforming working hours that read like a declaration of war against the CDU. "Self-determination, Not Deregulation" is the title of the seven-page document that was signed by the SPD working group on labor, the youth organization Jusos, the "60plus" working group and the women's wing of the SPD.

In the paper, the Social Democrats not only reiterate the points that already appeared in Bas' draft back in June. They also demand that, in the future, employers and employees should decide on working hours "jointly and by mutual agreement." They argued that it is not "in the spirit of a modern reform of working time law" if only employers can determine when employees finish work.

From a political perspective, the dispute over reforming work hours has long become more than just a debate over legal provisions. It is a fundamental dispute over how much flexibility workers should be expected to tolerate in the future and to what extent the state should protect them. And it is yet another stumbling block for the already beleaguered government in Berlin.

This article was translated from German.

entries.title: France reports more than 1,800 arrests after riots, looting and arson during cost-of-living protests
entries.summary: Rioters torched public buildings and looted shops across France, destroying Limoges' historic town hall. The violence erupted during nationwide cost-of-living protests.
entries.content:
France

France: Over 1,800 arrested after looting, arson during protests

October 18, 2026

Rioters torched public buildings and looted shops across France, destroying Limoges' historic town hall. The violence erupted during nationwide cost-of-living protests.

More than 1,800 people were arrested across France following riots, looting and arson during cost-of-living protests, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said Sunday.

The unrest on Saturday has sharpened tensions ahead of France's 2027 presidential election, as anger over living costs collides with tight limits on government spending.

What happened during the protests?

Clashes, fires and looting broke out in several cities during Saturday's demonstrations. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said 150 police officers had been injured and blamed what he described as a highly organized, violent far-left group.

Paris police reported 855 arrests, describing the figure as a record. Prosecutors said 517 people remained in custody, including 171 minors. Those figures were provisional, with arrests continuing until early Sunday.

Most arrests in the capital were linked to suspected handling of stolen goods, participation in a group intending to commit violence, and vandalism.

In central France, rioters set fire to Limoges' historic town hall, leaving much of it gutted. Mayor Guillaume Guerin condemned the destruction.

"There are no words to condemn what happened, so appalling is it," he told broadcaster LCI. "The country is in chaos."

Authorities reported attacks on public buildings and shops in Marseille, Lyon, Avignon and Grenoble. Police used tear gas, batons and water cannon in several cities.

Demonstrators were also reported injured. The newspaper Le Figaro reported that a 17-year-old lost a hand to a grenade fired by police in Saint-Étienne.

What have leading French politicians said?

President Emmanuel Macron vowed that those responsible would be prosecuted and punished.

"No room for violence in our Republic," he wrote on X, condemning attacks on government buildings, businesses and town halls.

Opposition politicians seeking to succeed Macron in presidential elections in April and May also responded to the unrest.

Far-right candidate Marine Le Pen accused the party of her far-left rival Jean-Luc Melenchon of having "legitimized the violence." She pledged to protect the French "from the violence of the extreme left."

Melenchon, who had backed the demonstrations and preceding student protests, urged demonstrators to stay away from looting, calling it "contrary to our methods."

The demonstrations brought together grievances over fuel prices, low wages and problems facing farmers and firefighters. School and university students demanding better learning conditions also participated.

The interior ministry put nationwide turnout at 550,000, including 110,000 in Paris. The CGT trade union gave a higher national estimate of 800,000.

France's high debt and budget deficit limit the government's ability to meet demands for additional spending.

Online calls to revive the yellow vest movement have added to government concerns that student demonstrations could grow into broader unrest.

The yellow vest movement began in 2018 over planned fuel tax increases and grew into wider protests over living costs and inequality. Named after the high-visibility vests worn by demonstrators, it brought months of nationwide demonstrations, some marked by violent clashes with police.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: Vietnam signs free trade deal with four European countries
entries.summary: Vietnam has signed a deal with four non-EU members that covers trade in goods and services, intellectual property rights, and sustainable development, among other areas.
entries.content:
October 18, 2026

Vietnam has signed a deal with four non-EU members that covers trade in goods and services, intellectual property rights, and sustainable development, among other areas.

Vietnam and four European countries signed a free trade agreement in Hanoi on Sunday.

The deal was announced by the governments of Vietnam and Norway.

Vietnam's Trade Ministry said it signed the deal with the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), which is made upNorway, Switzerland, Iceland and Liechtenstein.

The four European countries are not part of the European Union (EU).

The official talks between Vietnam and the EFTA began in 2012. The talks were interrupted in 2018 and only resumed last year.

How does the deal benefit Vietnam?

The agreement between Vietnam, which is Southeast Asia's fastest-growing economy, and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) waives or reduces customs duties, including on imports of industrial, fish and agricultural products.

Under the deal, around half of Norway's exports ​to ‌Vietnam will be tariff-free, with more than 98% ‌to be tariff-free within seven ‌years, ​the Norwegian government said in a statement.

According to the signing parties, the deal covers trade in goods and services, intellectual property rights, trade remedies and sustainable development, among other areas, both parties say.

Last year, the trade value between the EFTA and Vietnam stood at €4.8 billion ($5.4 billion), according to the association.

Vietnam said the agreement showed the parties' resolve to "reinforce the rules-based trading system amid continued volatility in the global economy," according to a government statement.

It was also expected to help Vietnam "diversify its import and export markets" and "integrate more deeply into global value chains," the government said.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: How reliant is Ukraine on the US-controlled Starlink internet service?
entries.summary: Kyiv keeps issuing warnings that the satellite internet system Starlink is being restricted in Ukraine. How dependent is the country on the system, and what would happen if it went down?
entries.content:
October 18, 2026

Kyiv keeps issuing warnings that the satellite internet system Starlink is being restricted in Ukraine. How dependent is the country on the system, and what would happen if it went down?

Few technological systems have played such an important role in the war in Ukraine as Starlink, central to the communications, reconnaissance and drone operations of the Ukrainian armed forces. There are currently widespread concerns that Elon Musk's satellite internet service in Ukraine may be restricted or even switched off. In recent days, Kyiv has repeatedly reported disruptions and restrictions affecting its use.

How Starlink enables communications

Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, Ukraine has made extensive use of the satellite internet service, which is operated by the US company SpaceX. With it, military personell can continue to communicate and exchange data, even when infrastructure has been destroyed or cellphone networks are down.

According to the Center for Security Studies (CSS) at ETH Zurich, around 50,000 Starlink terminals were in use in Ukraine in 2025. These are the system's specialised receiving and transmitting devices, which enable communications on the battlefield. They are also used to relay orders between command levels and receive drone footage.

The importance of the Starlink network can in part be explained by events at the beginning of the war. According to a CSS analysis, the KA-SAT satellite system previously favored by Ukraine was targeted in a cyberattack just hours before Russia's invasion. Starlink quickly became a vital alternative.

Starlink and Starshield: civilian versus military use

When discussing current affairs, the terms "Starlink" and "Starshield" are often used interchangeably.

However, Starlink is SpaceX's commercial satellite internet service, whereas Starshield is specifically designed for governmental and military use. While based on the same technological infrastructure, it is designed for security and defense applications.

This distinction matters, because the latest reports of restrictions seem to primarily concern systems used for military purposes. Elon Musk recently stated that Starshield systems are controlled by the US government, whereas Starlink is a commercial service operated by SpaceX.

The role of Starlink in drone warfare

Alongside communications, Starlink is mainly used for drone operations. The system provides an internet connection for ground, naval and aerial drones.

This connection means video footage can be transmitted almost in real time, while drones can be controlled over long distances. Ukraine uses these systems for reconnaissance and attacks deep behind enemy lines.

According to ETH Zurich, images and GPS coordinates of Russian positions are also transmitted via these communication channels. The data is sent to artillery units and used to coordinate operations.

What throttling Starlink would mean

According to Ukrainian media reports, on Tuesday night, SpaceX temporarily introduced a speed restriction for Starlink terminals in Ukraine, limiting terminals in motion to a speed of about 160 kilometers per hour (100 mph).

Such a restriction has direct consequences for fast-moving Ukrainian drones, some of which travel at speeds of up to 300 kilometers per hour (186 mph). If the connection to the drone is lost, live video footage can no longer be transmitted, and the systems can no longer be controlled in real time. The drones effectively have to continue their mission while flying blind.

Restricting or even shutting down a Starlink network would therefore not only make communication more difficult. It would also affect Ukrainian drone operations, and other military activities.

More than just satellite internet

However, Starlink and its military counterpart, Starshield, are only one essential component of Ukraine's defense system. Ukraine also receives reconnaissance data from western partners, including information about Russian air attacks, missile launches, troop movements and anti-aircraft positions, as well as potential routes to avoid them.

This information helps with air defense and offensive operations. Without this intelligence, it would be significantly harder for Ukraine to carry out long-range drone operations against targets in Russian territory.

The two elements are particularly effective when combined. Reconnaissance data provides information about potential targets and routes, while Starlink ensures that this data can be quickly relayed to units.

This is why reports that the US is limiting access to its reconnaissance data are as worrying as the possibility that Starlink might be throttled. Other NATO countries, such as the United Kingdom and France, can also provide reconnaissance data, but not to the extent as the United States.

Strategic dependence

Europe has several alternatives to Starlink, including Eutelsat/OneWeb. However, their ability to match Starlink's performance in wartime conditions has not yet been tested on a large scale.

The recurrent concern about possible restrictions makes clear that satellite communications have become a central component of Ukrainian defense. And while relying on a single provider simplifies operations, it also shows how dependent modern armed forces have become on private technology companies. Experts say this marks a fundamental change in warfare.

Meanwhile, Ukraine's successful use of Starlink has helped the system to achieve global recognition.

This article has been translated from German.

entries.title: Populist Czech PM Babis goes empty-handed in Senate elections
entries.summary: Opposition parties still control the Czech Senate, in a major blow to Prime Minister Andrej Babis' and his governing coalition.
entries.content:
Czech Republic

Populist Czech PM Babis goes empty-handed in Senate elections

October 18, 2026

Opposition parties still control the Czech Senate, in a major blow to Prime Minister Andrej Babis' and his governing coalition.

The ruling coalition of populist billionaire Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis has failed to win a single seat in elections in the Senate.

The result means pro-Western opposition parties control the chamber, the upper house of parliament.

The election on Saturday was the first electoral test for Babis after he won parliamentary elections in October 2025 that returned him to power after a break of four years since his first term as premier.

What happened in the Czech Senate elections?

Final results from the two-day ballot showed that candidates directly linked to the opposition parties won 22 of the 27 seats up for grabs in the 81-member Senate, retaining a previous opposition majority.

The centrist ANO (or YES) movement led by Babis failed to win any more seats, leaving it with 14 Senate lawmakers.

Babis called the result "catastrophic."

"We certainly didn't expect that we wouldn't win a single Senate seat in this election," he said, but vowed to nonetheless go ahead with his government's agenda.

That includes an unpopular plan to revamp funding for the country’s public broadcasters.

His euroskeptic coalition has also ended direct military support for Ukraine as it defends itself against a Russian invasion, and opposed European Union policies to combat global warming.

Although the lower house of the Czech parliament plays the main legislative role, the Senate has a big say in passing constitutional amendments and approving Constitutional Court judges.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: India: CJP leader Abhijeet Dipke released after detention
entries.summary: Two other prominent CJP leaders are set to be released on Sunday. India has seen huge rallies calling on the country's top election official to step down over alleged manipulation of voter rolls.
entries.content:
Asia

India: 'Cockroach' leader Abhijeet Dipke released after detention

October 18, 2026

Two other prominent CJP leaders are set to be released on Sunday. India has seen huge rallies calling on the country's top election official to step down over alleged manipulation of voter rolls.

Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), was released on Saturday, a day after he was detained by the Delhi police during protests against the election authority in India.

The 31-year-old youth leader was detained while he was trying to join the protest rally which the CJP movement had called in the capital's central Connaught Place district.

The movement published a photo of him on X in which it referred to Dipke as "a free man."

"Abhijeet Dipke released," CJP legal affairs chief Ratna Singh said on social media.

Singh said Dipke was released after agreeing to certain conditions. She did not provide details about the terms.

In a post on Instagram, Dipke said he "knew going to jail was inevitable" and that he was ready to face "whatever comes my way."

"Because the day I decided to come back to India, I placed my fate in the hands of the people of India and the Constitution of this country."

What are the protests about?

All India Students' Association (AISA) President Neha Bora, who was also detained during a protest in New Delhi on Friday, was released later on Friday evening.

Bora has emerged as a prominent face in the protests against India's Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, over alleged manipulation of voter lists.

A widespread review exercise — called Special Intensive Revision (SIR) — has struck off over 130 million names from India's electoral rolls since it began last year.

Opposition leaders and critics say that those removed from the voter lists include a large proportion of minority voters. They accuse Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist BJP of using the exercise as a tool to secure future electoral gains.

The neutrality of the Election Commission of India (ECI) is also being questioned.

The ECI denies favoring any party. It says the SIR removes deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and also helps in preventing the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants."

Youth being made 'pawns' — BJP



Modi's party has slammed its opponents for undermining democracy and has denounced the protests as attempts to create "anarchy". 

BJP's Rajnath Singh — who is also India's defense minister — addressed the protests at a press conference on Friday.

Singh accused the opposition, led by the Congress party, of wanting to bring a "regime change along the lines of Bangladesh" and using Indian youth as "pawns in the politics of disorder."

"It appears that the Congress and its political allies, both directly and through their affiliated organisations, are attempting to channel the energy of young people not into constructive activities and nation-building, but into instruments of political confrontation and the spread of chaos," he said.

Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka's custody ends Sunday

Two other senior CJP leaders, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, were arrested on October 14 for entering Jantar Mantar.

Jantar Mantar had been a prominent protest site in the heart of Delhi for decades. However, Delhi police blocked it amid heavy barricading and deployment.

The two leaders were sent to five days of judicial custody, which ends Sunday. The CJP has warned of legal action if Das and Ranka are not released.

"Now just waiting for my brothers to be free", Dipke said in a post on X that included a photo of Ranka and Das.

For the latest coverage of news from India on Sunday, check out our blog.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: India news: Kolkata stampede dampens Durga Puja festivities
entries.summary: Authorities have detained several people over a deadly stampede in India's eastern city of Kolkata, after the state vowed strict action. Meanwhile, 'Cockroach' leader Dipke is out of detention. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

India news: Kolkata stampede dampens Durga Puja festivities

Published October 17, 2026last updated October 18, 2026

Authorities have detained several people over a deadly stampede in India's eastern city of Kolkata, after the state vowed strict action. Meanwhile, 'Cockroach' leader Dipke is out of detention. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

Here's our coverage from India on Saturday and Sunday, October 17 and 18:

  • A stampede at a festival in Kolkata kills at least 17 people and injures 25 others
  • Kolkata police detains festival organizers, Home Minister Amit Shah to visit victims
  • Truck hits devotees in Gwalior, kills at least 13
  • India's 'Cockroach' movement founder Abhijeet Dipke released a day after his detention over a fresh protest call in the capital
  • Student leader Neha Bora also released from detention
  • Six US lawmakers urge Marco Rubio to bring up India protest crackdown during his upcoming visit

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Kolkata police issues prohibitory order after stampede

Kolkata police issues prohibitory order after stampede

Authorities in the city of Kolkata have imposed restrictions in the area around Chor Bagan after a stampede at a Durga Puja pandal killed at least 19 people.

The order prohibits gatherings of five people or more, processions, public meetings, slogans or public speeches. It will remain in place until October 20.

Similar instructions were imposed in central Delhi and other cities during protests led by India's Cockroach movement.

In a notification announcing the order, Kolkata police said it had received intelligence warning of a possible law and order problem, news agency ANI reported.

Earlier on Sunday, the city's police formally arrested seven people in connection with the stampede at the Chorbagan Sarbojonin Durgotsab Samity Durga Puja pandal.

As per Indian media, at least 19 people have died due to the crush on Saturday evening and several others remain in critical condition.

Skip next section Truck hits devotees in Gwalior, kills at least 13

Truck hits devotees in Gwalior, kills at least 13

At least 13 people were killed and 40 others injured on Sunday morning in India's central city of Gwalior, authorities said, after an out-of-control truck hit a crowd of devotees.

Indian media reported that the truck, loaded with paddy, broke through police barricades before it lost control and crashed into a temple's outer wall and gate. The incident occurred around 1:30 a.m. local time Sunday (2000 GMT Saturday).

Gwalior Senior Superintendent of Police told News agency ANI that the incident occurred in an area where heavy vehicles are restricted. Of the injured, five to six people were in a critical condition.

An eyewitness told ANI that they saw some people die on the spot. "The truck was overloaded; it came suddenly and ran over some shops and people. My brother also sustained injuries," the witness said. Others complained of delayed assistance and confused Information on treatment.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said he was "distressed" to learn about the "mishap," announcing monetary compensation for the next of kin to each of those who lost their lives.

"I express my deepest condolences to the bereaved families and pray for the swift recovery of those injured," Indian President Droupadi Murmu said on social media.

India, with 1.4 billion people, recorded more than 183,000 road traffic deaths in 2025, or over 500 a day, according to the roads ministry.

The temple in question was devoted to an Indian Goddess, Sheetla Mata, who is revered for her healing powers and her association with relief from fever and disease.

Her devotees conduct certain ceremonies in the early hours of the morning when temperatures are cool. Her worship typically focuses on practices such as cold food offerings and avoiding use of fire.

Skip next section Kolkata stampede: Police detain 12, chief minister vows strict action

Kolkata stampede: Police detain 12, chief minister vows strict action

Police in India's eastern metropolitan city of Kolkata detained 12 people on Saturday night, including the organizers of Chor Bagan Durga Puja, as they probe a stampede that killed nearly 20 people.

The latest update from the state's Chief Minister's X account puts the death toll at 17, with another 25 injured. However, Indian media, including news agency Press Trust of India (PTI), reported that at least 19 people had died.

The detentions came after West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari promised strict action against those who failed to carry out their duties to maintain crowd safety.

"We have detained 12 people in connection with our probe into the Chor Bagan incident. Our officers are talking to them to find out the cause that led to today's mishap. If any lapses are found, we will act as per the law," the officer told PTI.

Meanwhile, the West Bengal government has announced an independent investigation into the matter, led by a sitting judge of the city's high court.

"We will check the footage and take appropriate measures against those who failed to manage the crowd. That could be a member of the puja committee, a homeguard, a temporary worker, a policeman, or a private company security guard. Nobody will be spared," Adhikari said.

The politics of Durga Puja

Stampedes at religious and cultural festivals are not uncommon in India, but Adhikari's government is under pressure to make the city's biggest annual festival a hit this year.

Adhikari belongs to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's right-wing Bharatiya Janata Party which won the state elections in West Bengal for the first time in India's history, ending former Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee's 15-year rule there.

The festive season was facing pressure even before it began. Food and fuel inflation, worsened by the conflict in the Middle East and lower than normal rainfall at home, is eating into people's disposable incomes. 

Amit Shah, India's Union Home Minister — and Modi's right-hand man — is set to visit the victims and their family members on Sunday morning. The minister had arrived in Kolkata on Saturday evening for a series of festive programs which have now been postponed.

Skip next section Welcome back to our coverage

Welcome back to our coverage

Good morning! and welcome back to DW's weekend coverage on India.

This is Mahima Kapoor reporting from Studio Delhi to relieve Dharvi from her shift as she takes off for a well-deserved vacation.

Dharvi isn't the only one stepping away from her desk as India kicked off its festive season last week. We're currently in the middle of Navratri and Durga Puja, festivals celebrating the different forms of the Indian Goddess Durga.

Navratri — which translates roughly to 'nine nights' — is fervently celebrated across north and western India with colorful dances and vegetarian delicacies. In the east, Durga Puja takes on an artistic fervor, where numerous beautiful tents are set up to welcome the Goddess back to her maternal home.

They herald the countdown to India's biggest festival of the year, Diwali.

But the festive cheer has been dampened, at least temporarily, in the eastern state of West Bengal.

On Saturday evening, heavy crowds, rain and inadequate safety measures led to a stampede in the city fo Kolkata, killing over a dozen people and injuring several more.

Stay tuned for updates on that and more from India on Sunday.

Skip next section Many killed in stampede at religious festival in Kolkata

Many killed in stampede at religious festival in Kolkata

At least 17 people, including 13 women and a child, were killed in a stampede at the Durga Puja religious festival in North Kolkata that was likely caused by sudden rainfall.

"Today (17/10/26), at around 19:40 hrs, a stampede occurred at the exit gate of the Sarada Park (Chor Bagan) Puja Pandal in the Girish Park Police Station area due to heavy crowds of pandal visitors amid rain," the Kolkata Police said in a statement, adding that the injured were taken to the hospital.

West Bengal's Chief Minister Suvendhu Adhikari told reporters that the fatalities included a seven-year-old girl and that 25 others were injured in a stampede.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi called the incident "extremely distressing" and announced interim compensation for the families of those who died.

The largest annual Hindu festival in India's eastern state of West Bengal, Durga Puja attracts thousands of devotees to temporary structures called pandals that house idols of the goddess Durga.

Poor management and safety lapses at large events in India, such as religious festivals, often result in deadly crowd incidents. A stampede at last year's Kumbh Mela religious fair killed 30 people and injured several others.

Skip next section CJP founder released a day after detention

CJP founder released a day after detention

Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), was released by an Indian court on Saturday, one day after his detention for attempting to lead a protest rally in New Delhi.

The movement published a photo of him on X in which it referred to Dipke as "a free man."

The CJP's head of legal affairs, Ratna Singh, said Dipke was released after agreeing to certain conditions. She did not provide details about the terms.

Neha Bora, a prominent student activist and the face of the protests, was also detained on Friday while attempting to reach central Delhi with dozens of supporters. She was released earlier on Saturday.

For more, head over to our report on Dipke and Bora's release.

Skip next section WATCH — Indians in Germany protest as voter roll controversy goes global

WATCH — Indians in Germany protest as voter roll controversy goes global

India's youth-led Cockroach Janta Party is challenging the Indian Election Commission over alleged electoral irregularities.

The controversy is spilling beyond India's borders. Indians in Berlin are joining calls for accountability over controversial voter list revisions.

Skip next section Supreme Court says access to internet fundamental right for children, calls blanket bans 'disproportionate'

Supreme Court says access to internet fundamental right for children, calls blanket bans 'disproportionate'

India's top court declared that access to and use of the internet is a fundamental right of every individual, including children, legal news outlet LiveLaw reported Saturday.

It said that a blanket ban on children's internet activity could make them vulnerable to greater risks rather than protect them from online abuse and exploitation. 

The Supreme Court also issued directions to bolster the processes for detecting and removing child sexual exploitation and abuse material (CSEAM) from social media and other online platforms, the report said. 

The court stressed that the right to freedom of speech and expression also incorporates the right to know, receive and impart information and ideas, LiveLaw reported.

The two-judge bench described the internet as a "marketplace of ideas, creative expression and information" and said that its value went beyond the material it contains, as it provides opportunities for children in remote areas and those with disabilities.

"For many children, particularly in remote areas, it is often the only source of learning and information," the court said, according to LiveLaw.

For children with special needs, the internet is often the only platform where they can find company with others like them, the court said.

The court acknowledged that the internet, in its current form, poses safety risks to children. But it said that keeping children away from the internet because of failures by platforms and the relevant authorities to detect and remove harmful content would amount to mistaking the victim for the problem, LiveLaw reported.

What did the court say on blanket restrictions on internet use for children?

The Supreme Court said that a legal ban would not stop children from using the internet, and that they could move to other unregulated platforms.

"Any blanket restriction on the access of internet by children is nothing more than unproven measures of proven disproportionality," LiveLaw cited the court as saying.

The Supreme Court called for safeguards to ensure online child safety and the regulation of content accessible to children.

It suggested measures such as a "child mode" for social media accounts, LiveLaw said.

Saturday's Supreme Court judgement comes amid a global debate on the ban of social media for children over risks from harmful content. Australia declared the world's first social media ban for  under-16s last year.

France followed suit this summer, before its Constitutional Court blocked the move.

Skip next section US lawmakers urge Marco Rubio to bring up India protest crackdown

US lawmakers urge Marco Rubio to bring up India protest crackdown

Six lawmakers from the United States' Democratic Party have called on US Secretary of State Marco Rubioto raise India's handling of the youth protests during his visit next week. 

The US representatives include Pramila Jayapal, Ilhan Omar, Jim McGovern, Rashida Tlaib, Eleanor Holmes Norton, and Jesus Garcia.

"As the world's largest democracies, the US and India have an obligation to promote and defend the rights to freedom of assembly and expression," Jayapal wrote on X, sharing a letter addressed to Rubio.

The letter alleges a "pattern of repression, wrongful detention, and excessive use of force by security forces" during the student protests in Delhi and other parts of the country.

The lawmakers also highlight incidents of "apparent surveillance," saying that they had received reports that the Indian diplomatic missions in the US "hired photographers to surveil protesters on American soil."

"These incidents raise particular alarm in light of India's documented pattern of engaging in transnational repression, including through the weaponization of consular services, harassment, intimidation, and physical violence," the letter said.

The group urged Rubio to prioritize the issues in his discussion with Indian officials.

The US Secretary of State is visiting India early next week, after traveling to Uzbekistan.

He is slated to meet Indian foreign minister S Jaishankar in Mumbai. His agenda also shows a trip to Jamnagar in the western state of Gujarat.

Skip next section Student leader Neha Bora released from detention

Student leader Neha Bora released from detention

All India Students' Association (AISA) President Neha Bora, who was also detained during the latest protest in New Delhi on Friday was released later in the night.

Bora has emerged as a prominent face in the protests against India's top poll official.

Speaking to the media after her release, Bora called for Dipke and other protesters to be released, saying that they had been "illegally detained".

"They are ordinary citizens demanding accountability and their right to vote. Carrying out such illegal detentions and keeping people at the police station overnight makes no sense at all," Bora said.

For more on Bora's release, and that of other protest leaders including Abhijeet Dipke, head over to our report.

Skip next section CJP's Dipke arrested after detention — reports

CJP's Dipke arrested after detention — reports

Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) Founder Abhijeet Dipke has been arrested, following his detention on Friday when he stepped out to participate in a rally he had called in New Delhi, media reports said.

Dipke was arrested to ‌prevent a ⁠breach ⁠of the peace and will be taken before a Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) court later today, news agencies ANI and PTI reported.

CJP legal affairs head Ratna Singh also said that Dipke had been arrested, adding that he would appear before the SEM court in central Delhi's Mandir Marg at 12 p.m. (630 UTC).

Singh claimed that Dipke's lawyers had not met him.

The 'Cockroach' movement said early on Saturday that they did not know where their founder had been detained, calling his detention a "kidnapping."

"Until now, neither his parents nor his lawyers and not the CJP team have been given any updates about his location," the CJP said on X, as it published a video of CJP leader Ajinkya Shinde asking about Dipke's whereabouts.

Dipke was detained publicly on Friday as he left the house in Jhandewalan where he was staying to take part in CJP's 'Lehra Do Tiranga' (Wave the tricolor) protest rally in Connaught Place.

Videos of his detention showed the CJP founder being told by a police official that he was being placed under "preventive detention" before he was taken to a police car.

Dipke was seen displaying India's flag as police and media personnel surrounded him. Some supporters were seen trying to block the police vehicle from driving away with Dipke.

Just hours earlier, a group of Delhi Police officials had visited the 31-year-old at the Jhandewalan residence and served him a notice barring the Friday protest.

The Delhi Police had previously reiterated that Section 163 of India's criminal procedure law, which prohibits any form of assembly or protest, was in force in the Connaught Place area.

"The manner in which he was picked up from right outside his residence, no information about his whereabouts, and the fact that even his lawyers have been unable to meet him raise serious concerns about due process and fundamental rights," Singh wrote on X.

Even after Dipke's detention, hundreds of protesters turned up in Connaught Place defying the heavy security deployment. The protesters were seen waving the Indian national flag as part of the CJP's 'Tricolor' rally. According to police, some 150 protesters were detained during the demonstrations.

The fresh protests came after CJP co-conveners Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das were sent to a five-day detention in jail on Wednesday for alleged violation of prohibitory orders and breach of a peace bond after they attempted a demonstration. They too were carrying the Indian tricolor and the flag has since been at the center of CJP's campaign.

The Indian flag "belongs to the 1.3 billion people of this country and not the Delhi police. We will wave it where we want!" the movement has said.

Dipke, Das and Ranka were earlier detained on October 10 from a plane as they arrived in the capital for a protest march calling for the resignation of India's Chief Election Commionser Gyanesh Kumar over alleged manipulation of voter lists.

They were released after nearly 24 hours.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's studio in New Delhi, bringing you the weekend edition of the India blog, where we break down all the biggest headlines that are creating a buzz in the country.

The world's largest democracy has seen almost daily protests since the start of October. The youth-led 'Cockroach' movement, opposition parties, student organizations and civil society members are calling for India's election chief to step down over a sweeping revision of voter rolls that they say benefits Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

On Friday, another protest called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) at a key business district in the heart of Delhi culminated in detentions. 

CJP Founder Abhijeet Dipke was taken away in a police car even before he could get to the protest location. It was the second time that Dipke was detained in less than a week. 

Reports now say that the 'Cockroach' founder has been arrested following his detention, and is due to appear before a Special Executive Magistrate court today.

With protests being prohibited and demonstrations ending in detentions, the stir over accountability and electoral reform has also sparked a debate over the public's right to protest.

Meanwhile, a group of Democratic lawmakers in the US have called on Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is visiting India next week, to raise with Indian officials the alleged wrongful detentions and excessive use of force during the student protests in New Delhi and other parts of the country.

Stay with us as we bring you all this and more.

entries.title: Canada: Major fire reported at military base in Alberta
entries.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has said a "serious incident" sparked a major fire at a military base in Alberta. He did not provide details on the cause of the fire.
entries.content:
Canada

Canada: Major fire reported at military base in Alberta

October 18, 2026

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has said a "serious incident" sparked a major fire at a military base in Alberta. He did not provide details on the cause of the fire.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Saturday said a "serious incident" sparked a major fire at a military base in Alberta.

"A serious incident creating a major fire has occurred at CFB Wainwright, in Alberta," Carney said in a post on X.

He added that the federal government was working closely with Alberta officials and local authorities. 



Defense Minister David McGuinty later confirmed that there have been "fatalities and injuries" as a result of the incident on the base.



Located about 180 kilometers (112 miles) southeast of Edmonton, Alberta's capital, Canadian Forces Base Wainwright is one of the country's busiest military training bases.

What else do we know about the major fire in Alberta?

The Municipal District of Wainwright said the fire was spreading rapidly due to high winds.

"The fire south of Wainwright crossed the base fence earlier today and is being actively managed ... Emergency crews remain focused on protecting life safety, homes, and other structures," it said.



Alberta Premier Danielle Smith called the fire "significant and tragic" and said many military personnel are affected.

"We are learning of a significant and tragic fire at CFB Wainwright today that is affecting many of our brave military personnel," Smith said in a post on social media.

The incident occurred just days before people in Alberta, home to the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves, will vote in the October 19 referendum on whether the province wants to begin the process of separating from the rest of Canada.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: 'No Kings' rallies push early voting ahead of US midterm elections
entries.summary: Organizers of the "No Kings" protests, known for their anti-Trump sentiment, are urging Americans to vote early in the November 3 midterm elections, as Republicans face tough races to retain control of Congress.
entries.content:
United States of America

'No Kings' rallies push early voting ahead of US midterm elections

October 18, 2026

Organizers of the "No Kings" protests, known for their anti-Trump sentiment, are urging Americans to vote early in the November 3 midterm elections, as Republicans face tough races to retain control of Congress.

Protesters gathered across the United States for the latest "No Kings" demonstrations as Americans begin casting ballots ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.

Dubbed "No Kings: Vote Early," Saturday's event aimed to fire up Americans to vote early in the midterm elections, which will determine which party controls Congress, rather than protest against President Donald Trump and his administration.

"It's a day of nonpartisan voter participation: we are bringing our community together to make a plan to vote early and ensuring every eligible voter understands their options for how to vote and has the opportunity to make their voice heard," organizers said in a statement.

Most areas of the United States allow voters to cast their ballots ahead of time, sometimes weeks in advance.

Trump opposes mail-in voting

Trump repeatedly criticized mail-in voting and sought to restrict the practice ahead of the midterms. He regularly votes by mail-in ballot, arguing that his job makes him an exception to his criticism of the practice. 

The US president blamed election fraud, without providing evidence, for his defeat in the 2020 presidential election against Democrat Joe Biden.

Various surveys have concluded that restricting mail-in ballots could benefit Republicans, as Democratic voters disproportionately use the system to cast their ballots.

Opponents fear that the Trump administration may try to interfere with the midterm results, particularly if Republicans lose the majority.

Opinion polls suggest Democrats are poised to regain control of the House ​of Representatives, while the Senate remains too close to call.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Ilhan Omar: The US Democrat targeted by Donald Trump
entries.summary: Donald Trump has described her as "garbage" and a "criminal" who does nothing but "bitch." Congress member Ilhan Omar has long been the target of angry verbal attacks from the US president. But why her?
entries.content:
United States of America

Ilhan Omar: The US Democrat targeted by Donald Trump

October 17, 2026

Donald Trump has described her as "garbage" and a "criminal" who does nothing but "bitch." Congress member Ilhan Omar has long been the target of angry verbal attacks from the US president. But why her?

"Ilhan Omar, whatever the hell her name is, with the little – with the little turban, I love her. She comes in, does nothing but bitch."

"Ilhan Omar is garbage. She's garbage. Her friends are garbage. […] These aren't people that work. These aren't people that say, let's go. Come on, let's make this place great. These are people that do nothing but complain."

"She comes in from a country without laws, without police, without military, where all they do is shoot each other. And she comes into our country, and she says, 'I have a constitutional right.' She's telling us about the constitution, and she comes from one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet."

These are just three of Donald Trump's many attacks on US Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar. Few people have been targeted as ferociously by the US president. But why has Trump singled her out for such hostility?

Who is Ilhan Omar?

Ilhan Abdullahi Omar, 44, was born in Mogadishu, the capital of Somalia. She fled the civil war in the country while still a child, and spent four years in a refugee camp in Kenya. She finally came with her family to the US in 1995, at the age of 12, and became a US citizen in 2000. She joined the Democratic Party, and made a career as a politician on the party's left wing. Since January 2019, she has served as representative for the state of Minnesota and one of the first two Muslim women to enter the US Congress.

Ilhan Omar is a practising Muslim who wears a hijab, and Congress altered a 180-year-old rule for her that prohibited head coverings in the chamber of the House of Representatives. Politically and socially, Omar champions progressive values, and often makes a connection between her faith and her commitment to social justice, human rights, and the protection of minorities.

Omar campaigns on issues such as universal health insurance, increasing the minimum wage, climate protection, and the cancellation of student debt. She is also one of Donald Trump's most prominent and outspoken critics, repeatedly accusing him of racism and systematically fomenting hatred against minorities, immigrants, and Muslims. She has frequently condemned raids by the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency (ICE), which she describes as a "militarized campaign of fear." She has also accused the president of corruption in office.

Criticism of Israel and accusations of antisemitism

Young, outspoken, female, Muslim, and a left-wing Democrat – politically, Ilhan Omar is almost the polar opposite of the 80-year-old Republican Trump. But she is also a controversial figure within her own party.

Omar is one of the fiercest critics of Israel in US politics, and has repeatedly called Washington's support for the country into question. She has been accused of antisemitism, and of supporting the movement BDS (Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions), which encourages people to boycott Israeli businesses. Omar has defended BDS as a legitimate form of non-violent protest and freedom of expression. In 2019, she even introduced a resolution in the US Congress that aimed to strengthen the right of Americans to boycott, with a view to countering laws that restrict what the BDS movement can do.

In early 2023, Republicans removed her from the House Foreign Affairs Committee over a number of controversial tweets, including a comment she made in 2021 that seemed to equate the actions of the US and Israel with those of the Taliban in Afghanistan, and the Palestinian group Hamas. The latter is classified as a terrorist organization by the US and many other countries around the world.

Accusations of embezzlement and immigration fraud

Her critics also tried to link Omar to a corruption scandal in her home state of Minnesota. During the COVID-19 pandemic, around $250 million (€220 million) were misappropriated from a government-funded food program for children. Omar had previously called for the rules of the program to be eased.

Many of those convicted were from the state's Somali community, something that political opponents, including Trump, seized on to claim Omar was involved. No law enforcement authorities have ever accused her of any wrongdoing.

The most recent accusation against Omar concerns her immigration to the US. For years, her opponents have claimed that she made false statements during the procedure, even alleging that she entered into a fraudulent marriage with her biological brother to help him secure a US visa. On October 12, federal officials ordered a search of Omar's home, investigating allegations that Omar's father lied about her age on her immigration application.

Controversial house search

Omar has repeatedly denied the accusations, describing them as part of a "campaign of political intimidation" and "an attempt to target political enemies." Several leading Democratic politicians have come to her defense, accusing the Trump administration of weaponizing the Justice Department and Department of Homeland Security against its political opponents.

Former immigration officials told the Reuters news agency that it is extremely unusual for a house search to be conducted as part of such an investigation, as the government should already have all the relevant immigration documents.

Many see a raid on the home of a sitting member of Congress over a formality from 26 years ago as excessive, and have been especially critical of the timing of the raid, just three weeks before the Congressional elections in which Omar is standing for re-election.

The long-standing, unwritten "60-Day Rule" holds that authorities do not take any public action against political candidates in the two months before an election, so as not to influence the outcome. Critics see the fact that this practice has been ignored in Omar's case as amounting to election interference.

Other Muslim politicians also targeted

With the midterm electionslooming, Trump is battling with plummeting approval ratings, and Omar is not the only Muslim politician the president has been attacking. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate in the Senate election in Michigan, is another.

At a rally last Saturday in Tennessee, Trump said of El-Sayed: "I call him Mohammed. Somebody said, 'His name isn't Mohammed, it's Abdul.' I said, 'To me, it's Mohammed.' I'm the president. I can call him whatever the hell I want. To me, he's Mohammed, and he's a radical jihadist."

There is no intelligence whatsoever to suggest that El-Sayed has any extremist connections. The 41-year-old epidemiologist was born and brought up in Michigan. He went to university there, then won a Rhodes scholarship to Oxford, where he gained a doctorate in public health. For many years, he was the health director of the city of Detroit. Like Omar, he too belongs to the progressive left wing of the US Democratic Party.

During the election campaign, El-Sayed has repeatedly emphasized that he is not the one responsible for the rise in food prices, the expensive rents, and other political grievances. He has placed the blame squarely on what he describes as the failed policies of the administration in Washington.

This article has been translated from German.
